messages.subject: Modified Robust Design in JAGS?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am a bit stuck at the moment and was hoping for a little feedback.  I have been trying to take Bailey's modified robust design (2004) fit originally with a modified version of MSSURVIV and get it to work in JAGS by extending the state-space multistate model in Kery and Schaub (2012).

I am working with a photo capture recapture vernal pool salamander dataset where multiple pools were drift fenced and salamanders were captured (photo taken), released inside the pool to breed and then captured again (photo taken) leaving the pool (if they didn't die breeding).  The dataset also contains a count of the number of metamorphs emerging from each pool the following spring.  So, I have a fecundity rate or average metamoprhs per female if I can control for detection and perhaps survival at the pool.

Detection is fairly high with few individuals getting past the drift fence without being captured but prior to matching the 14,000 photos I ended up screening some photos which had significant distortion due to photo glare.  I used Amphident, a photo matching software that converts photos to a coarsened red/black image which allows you to see how distorted an image is due to photo glare.  So, detection for me is potentially a bit lower especially in earlier years of the study when photo quality was not great.

The model is a bit complicated due to the fact that females "skip" breeding so you have a multi state model with an observable and unobservable state.   You also have two different intervals.  This includes a breeding interval between those secondary occasions when some subset of the females are at the pool breeding and a non-breeding interval when all individuals are in the surrounding upland forest.

Since you have no information on individuals in the unobservable state you have to constrain survival of unobservable individuals to be the same as individuals in the observable state during the non-breeding period.  Also, individuals can transition between states only during the non-breeding interval.

Other issues are differing interval lengths by year/pool due to females brooding eggs until a pool fills with water which differs year to year and pool to pool.

Right now I think I am simulating data that mimic my real data, but when I fit the models in JAGS the estimates of survival and state transition are biased.

I potentially have just made a mistake or two in my state transition or detection matrices or perhaps this state-space format JAGS is not feasible.   I would be grateful to anyone providing some advice to help me move forward.  I think the model would be applicable to herp data such as mine and beyond.

I attached my current code for simulating capture histories and fitting the JAGS model.

best,
Kris

messages.subject: Ecological Forecasting Outstanding Publication Award -- Applications due on March 1
messages.subject_clean: Ecological Forecasting Outstanding Publication Award -- Applications due on March 1
messages.body_plain:
**Please circulate this email widely**

The ESA Statistical Ecology Section's new Ecological Forecasting Outstanding Publication Award will be running its first competition this year. Applications are due to Mike Dietze (die...@bu.edu) by March 1. Details about the award and the nomination procedure can be found below and on the section's website <http://www.esa.org/stats/?page_id=54>.

Elise Zipkin

Section Chair

_____________________________________________________

Ecological Forecasting Outstanding Publication Award.

Background:

This award will be given annually in recognition of an outstanding scholarly publication (peer reviewed journal article, book chapter, or book) published within the last three years in the emerging field of Ecological Forecasting. The scope of the award is broad, spanning any ecological system, process, and spatiotemporal scale.It encompasses research, both basic and applied, that generates predictions or projections, or which advances forecasting methods, tools, theories, or concepts.

Eligibility and how to apply:

Nominations are open to all career stages, and self nominations are permitted, but in all cases the lead author must be a member of the Ecological Society of America. Eligible papers must be peer-reviewed with a publication date on or after January 1 three years prior to the current deadline (e.g. papers for the March 2018 deadline need to have been published after Jan 1, 2015). Papers in press will also be considered but must be publicly available (e.g., online early). Please note the date of acceptance and date the paper became available publicly in the cover letter for papers in press.

Nominations should include a PDF copy of the paper and a brief (< 1 page) cover letter highlighting the paper’s contribution to, and impact on, ecological forecasting. Materials should be sent to the Award's Committee Chair, Mike Dietze (die...@bu.edu), in an email with subject heading "Ecological ForecastingAward". The annual deadline for the nominations will be March 1, with the first competition taking place in 2018.

Award details:

The award winner will will receive a prize of $200 and recognition on the ESA Stats Ecology website <http://www.esa.org/stats/?page_id=54>. The winner will be announced at the annual Statistical Ecology Section social at the ESA annual meeting.

messages.subject: Introductory NIMBLE Workshop, Switzerland, April 2018
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we would also very much welcome a couple more people signing up for our exciting 3-day NIMBLE workshop which Perry de Valpine (UC  Berkeley) will be teaching in late April; see email below and also here: http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=3586.

Best regards ---  Marc Kéry

From: Kery Marc
Sent: 09 January 2018 12:46
To: hmec...@googlegroups.com; unmarked
Subject: Introductory NIMBLE Workshop, Switzerland, April 2018

Dear all,

from 23-25 April 2018 Michael Schaub and I are hosting a Nimble introductory workshop taught by Perry de Valpine (University of California, Berkeley), see attachment and also here: http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=3586

Nimble is the latest member of the software family for fitting hierarchical models that uses the BUGS language to describe the model. In our opinion this is almost a prerequisite for wide adoption by ecologist and other non-statisticians. Nimble offers exciting capabilities to extend the functionality, customize the MCMC samplers and allows fitting of hierarchical models by likelihood methods.

Best regards  --- Marc Kéry
